title: From Main Street to Capitol Hill, the Case for Democracy’s Library
content:
At a time when free speech is under attack and the public record is fragile, supporters gathered in San Francisco on October 21 to celebrate the Internet Archive’s work to preserve knowledge for all through Democracy’s Library, an initiative to make government information accessible to everyone.

Watch Recording | View Event Photos

Nancy Pelosi, Speaker Emerita of the U.S. House of Representatives, and Robert Reich, former U.S. Secretary of Labor, were among those offering congratulations and encouragement to the Archive at the celebration of “Democracy’s Library: Tools for Participation.”

“Preserving the data is essential to a democracy,” Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi declared from the stage at the Funston Avenue headquarters. “Lincoln said, ‘Public sentiment is everything. With it, you can accomplish almost anything. Without it, practically nothing.’ But for public sentiment to prevail, you have to know—and we have to show them where they can find out.”

title: A Behind-the-Scenes Look at the Physical Archive
content:
Visitors who came to the open house at the Physical Archive in Richmond, California, on October 20 were curious. They wanted to learn about the range of items collected, the process of preservation, and the staff responsible for making it all happen. 

As people toured the space and observed the various media being saved, many also expressed support and reverence for the Internet Archive’s work to provide universal access to all knowledge.

VIEW PHOTOS FROM THE EVENT

“I really care about preservation and digital culture. Places like this are important to maintaining and building the society we want to live in,” said Sidney Le, a film archivist who now works in logistics, of his third visit to the Physical Archives. “It’s good to see that people here are taking seriously the idea of holding on to culture and preserving it.”

Liz Rosenberg, donations manager for the Archive, welcomed the crowd in Richmond and provided directions for the evening.

title: Internet Archive Honors Poynter and IRE for Preserving Local News Online
content:
As newsrooms across the United States close, years of reporting are at risk of disappearing. Stories documenting local elections, holding public officials accountable, investigating community problems and recording everyday life can become difficult or impossible to find when the news organizations that produced them shut down. Much of this reporting now exists only in digital formats, where it can be lost when websites go offline or archives are never created.

Local journalism captures the first draft of history in communities across the country. Preserving it means ensuring that future generations can understand not only what happened, but how communities responded, how decisions were made and how those decisions shaped people’s lives.

Two journalism organizations – the Poynter Institute and Investigative Reporters and Writers (IRE) – have stepped up to provide tools and training to preserve local news online.

For their work, the Internet Archive is honoring Poynter and IRE with the 2026 Internet Archive Hero Award.  The annual award recognizes individuals and organizations that have demonstrated leadership in making information available to people around the world.

title: Annual Celebration 2026: Street Fair to Showcase Internet Archive’s Projects and Allies
content:
Every year, the Internet Archive throws a party at our headquarters, celebrating a different facet of our ongoing preservation work. The theme for 2026 is “Democracy’s Library: Tools for Participation” and we’re putting a spotlight on the ways every day people can use our tools to participate through the Internet Archive—from saving and contributing materials to exploring government records, researching history, and building new tools with our collections and APIs. (NOTE: We have sold out of tickets for this event on Wednesday October 21).

This year, we will be featuring several of Internet Archive’s core projects in a street fair with live demos of our most impactful features. To begin, you can check out our Digitize a Book station, where you can try out our proven method of digitizing books, which we’ve been employing for 20 years that preservers the integrity of physical books.

title: Celebrating 2026 Internet Archive Artist in Residence: Christopher Burch
content:
Written by VITA HEWITT

“Echoes of Absence and Mythos: The Un-Archivists of Shitocracy” comes straight from the hands of artist Christopher Burch and opens on October 17 at Incline Gallery. Created in collaboration with the Internet Archive, D. Scott Miller, who wrote the Afro Surrealist Manifesto, and Incline Gallery, with funding from the San Francisco Arts Commission, this exhibition takes aim at the dual specters of societal erasure of Black experience and the often unmet need to amplify marginalized voices.

The Un-Archivists of Shitocracy, an imagined secret society comprised of those overlooked by history, takes these heavy subjects on through historical and contemporary contexts, mixed together with the hands of a trickster to challenge oppressive systems that seek to erase the narratives crucial to Black identity.
creator: Amir Saber Esfahani

title: Building the Hero Award: The Story Behind Taekyeom Lee’s 3D-Printed Model of the Internet Archive
content:
Taekyeom Lee is an educator, designer, maker, and researcher.

The associate professor of graphic design at Indiana University Bloomington is not only committed to teaching his students, Lee believes in sharing knowledge of art and design that inspires the broader community.

In 2021, Lee was an artist-in-residence at the Internet Archive in San Francisco. Fascinated by art featured in the Archive’s collection, he wanted to turn the works on the page and screen into a tactile experience.

Lee has built 3D printers based on the open-source project, RepRap. During the residency, he took a book about Korean ceramics published in 1966 from the archive’s collection, traced the shapes and turn them into 3D models, and built a DIY 3D Printer  to make physical small-scale vases out of clay. Lee documented the process and created a series of videos for others to replicate the machine to print clay with an open-source plan.

title: The People, Counted: Browse Raw Census Records at the Internet Archive
content:
The U.S. Census has been in the headlines lately, as proposed changes to the 2030 count have sparked debate over who gets counted and what information should be recorded as part of that process. Few government records say more about a democracy than the census, the once-a-decade count that decides who is represented in Congress, which makes it a natural fit for Democracy’s Library, the Internet Archive’s effort to make government information freely available to everyone. Thanks to the Allen County Public Library, the Internet Archive holds the U.S. Census collection. This collection contains digitized microfilm of the United States federal population census, 1790 to 1930 (minus the lost 1890 Census), and including the Indian Census rolls of 1885 to 1940, which were compiled by the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

The United States Census is one of the few institutional structures that was written into the Constitution, with Article I, Section 2 specifying that an “actual Enumeration” would be made every ten years in order to divide seats in the House of Representatives and direct taxes among the states.

title: Internet Archive to Demo Wayback Machine at Friday’s Uniqlo Street Festival
content:
The Internet Archive is joining other area nonprofits for the Uniqlo Street Festival on Friday, October 9, 2026, alongside the opening of Uniqlo’s new flagship store on Market Street. We’ll be set up with fellow San Francisco nonprofits Gray Area and the Exploratorium to help bring people and energy back to a part of the city that has sorely missed shoppers and foot traffic. We’ll be demoing the Wayback Machine, handing out stickers, and talking with attendees about digital preservation.

“Libraries have always found interesting ways to get in front of new audiences. More people than ever need to know about the valuable service of the Wayback Machine and why our digital culture should be preserved. People may be aware of the Internet Archive, but may not realize that we are also a San Francisco organization. This gives us an opportunity to meet with people in our community during this event,” said Merrilee Proffitt, director of Democracy’s Library US at the Internet Archive, who will be at the booth on Friday. “Plus, to be honest, I think many of us have a Uniqlo hoodie or two in our closets.”

title: Who Is Government Information For? Information Stewardship Forum 2026 Report
content:
Democracy’s Library exists as a project of the Internet Archive to make government publications and information broadly accessible and available. But Democracy’s Library is about more than collections – it is also about building community. 

In March 2026 the Internet Archive hosted the Information Stewardship Forum, a three-day convening that brought together 120 people working to preserve and provide access to United States government information. Participants came from libraries, archives, journalism, research, policy, philanthropy, nonprofits, and technology, and represented federal, state, and local parts of the government information ecosystem. We spent three days together discussing shared challenges and solutions as well as building community and connections.

We are pleased to share that a report from the event is now available. The report documents the methods used to design the meeting, what we heard, and shares results from the post event survey.

title: Internet Archive to Honor Poynter Institute and Investigative Reporters and Editors with 2026 Hero Award for Preserving Local News Online
content:
The Internet Archive is proud to announce that the Poynter Institute and Investigative Reporters and Editors (IRE) will receive the 2026 Internet Archive Hero Award for their leadership in preserving local news online.

The Internet Archive Hero Award recognizes individuals and organizations that have demonstrated leadership in making information available to people around the world. The Poynter Institute, a 50-year-old nonprofit that works to strengthen journalism and train journalists, and IRE, a member-driven nonprofit that has spent 50 years helping journalists do better investigative work, have made preservation a vital part of their work.

Local journalism is the first draft of history, and often the only record of what happened in a community. But as news increasingly moves online, that record is at risk. Stories can disappear when a newsroom closes, a website changes platforms, or digital archives are neglected. At the same time, major news publishers and media organizations are restricting access to web archiving tools like the Wayback Machine, making it harder to preserve the journalism being published today.
